detail.title: Complex Compliance Investigations

detail.abstract: Whether it is a financial institution like Wells Fargo, an automotive company like General Motors, a transportation company like Uber, or a religious organization like the Catholic Church, failing to properly prevent, detect, investigate, and remediate misconduct within an organization's ranks can have devastating results. The importance of the compliance function is accepted within corporations, but the reality is that all types of organizations-private or public-must ensure their members comply with legal and regulatory mandates, industry standards, and internal norms and expectations. They must police thousands of members' compliance with hundreds of laws. And when compliance failures occur at these complex organizations they can be significant and widespread in both scope and associated harms. Yet, careful examination and assessment reveals that many of the most significant and damning scandals occurring within organizations of late were entirely avoidable. Research within the field of corporate governance focuses on how firms are structured because those structures can result in better decision making within the firm. Structure refers to the manner of separating the work in an organization into subunits and dividing the control of and responsibilities for the work. The field of compliance relies heavily on these insights from corporate governance, which has led to a focus on what organizational structures will lead to compliance programs likely to prevent and detect misconduct within firms. When it comes time to investigate potential incidents of misconduct and determine whether they are material events, however, complex organizations must go beyond issues related to the best manner in which to structure a compliance program. Instead, this Article argues that firms must focus on process-based reforms-or the actions, practices, and routines firms employ to communicate and analyze informationthat will bolster a firm's “Complex Compliance Investigations” and act as a safety net when compliance programs fail to detect or appropriately respond to misconduct within firms.

title: Among high-income countries, how do national healthcare delivery systems compare when evaluated on total health expenditures and quality of care, and when considering which models the United States should adopt?

detail.title: Among high-income countries, how do national healthcare delivery systems compare when evaluated on total health expenditures and quality of care, and when considering which models the United States should adopt?
detail.abstract: The United States (US) dedicated nearly 18% of its gross domestic product (GDP) to healthcare in 2023- significantly higher than the 8-12% spent by other high-income countries. Despite this investment, data from the Peterson-KFF Health Tracker show that the US continues to underperform on several core public health indicators compared to peer nations. Understanding how other developed countries finance and deliver healthcare may therefore offer insights for improving US health outcomes. This literature review focuses on Canada, France, and the United Kingdom (UK), three countries with comparable spending patterns but differing approaches to healthcare financing and coverage. Their models provide important context for assessing which structural features the US might adopt. Longitudinal and observational studies consistently demonstrate that the US lags behind in major health indicators, including life expectancy, infant mortality, primary care availability, and rates of health insurance coverage. Canada, France, and the UK each operate single-payer universal coverage systems in which one primary payer- usually the government- finances healthcare for all residents. These models offer standardized, equitable coverage funded through taxation. In contrast, the US relies on a fragmented multi-payer system involving numerous private insurers alongside federal and state programs. This structure contributes to substantial gaps in coverage, particularly for individuals who cannot afford private insurance or who do not qualify for public programs. Ultimately, differences in healthcare efficiency distinguish the US from its peers. By examining how financing models influence national health outcomes, this review highlights pathways for improving the value and equity of US healthcare spending.

detail.title: Study Protocol: Prediction of Failure to Rescue in Hospitalised Adult Patients Using Models Based on Machine Learning and Process Mining
detail.abstract: BackgroundFailure to Rescue (FTR) is defined as the occurrence of clinical and/or functional deterioration that could potentially have been prevented through early detection and appropriate intervention. Early identification is essential for patient safety, as it is closely associated with quality of care and hospital mortality. Nevertheless, organisational and methodological limitations remain, hindering timely recognition and effective response. Overcoming these challenges requires optimising predictive algorithms and integrating clinical process management with the supporting information systems.ObjectiveTo design and validate predictive models based on machine learning and process mining to anticipate Failure to Rescue events in adult inpatient units.MethodsA retrospective observational study will be conducted based on electronic health records (EHRs) from Hospital Universitario de La Plana (La Plana University Hospital). The cohort will include all patients aged 18 years and older who were admitted between March 2023 and February 2024. Sociodemographic variables, care process-related variables, nursing assessments, laboratory parameters, and situations susceptible to FTR will be collected.
